description: Evaluates technical defenses against constructive liability in unlawful assembly cases, determining that neither a specific charge for rioting, an explicit overt act, nor the conviction of five specific individuals is mandatory, provided the underlying shared intent and required number of participants are factually established.
application_scenario: Use when an accused challenges their conviction for an offence read with Section 149 IPC by arguing they were not separately charged with rioting, committed no specific overt act, or that the acquittal of co-accused reduced the convicted group to fewer than five persons.
reasoning_flow: Ascertain whether the accused is charged with constructive liability under Section 149 IPC for an offence committed in prosecution of the common object of an unlawful assembly.

Reject any defense claiming the conviction is invalid solely because a distinct, separate charge under Section 147 or 148 IPC (rioting) was not formally framed, as those ingredients are implicitly subsumed.
Evaluate if the defense relies on the lack of a specific 'overt act'; hold that mere active presence sharing the common object (e.g., assembling with weapons) suffices for membership.

Assess if the number of convicted persons falls below the statutory minimum of five due to acquittals; uphold the application of Section 149 if the evidence proves that other unidentified or acquitted persons were factually present, making the assembly five or more.
example_application: An accused is convicted of murder under Section 302 read with 149 IPC despite being acquitted of rioting (Section 147) and only three people ultimately being convicted. The court upholds the conviction, noting that an overt act or a specific rioting charge is not required, and evidence showed the mob consisted of at least ten unidentified persons sharing the lethal common object.
shared_pattern: All three cases address defenses attempting to negate constructive liability under Section 149/147 IPC by pointing to missing procedural or numeric thresholds (no rioting charge, no overt act, less than five convicted), which the court rejects by looking at the substantive proof of the assembly and shared object.
scope_exclusions: Do not use for determining the substantive scope of the 'common object' itself or testing if a distinct secondary offense fell outside the assembly's shared intent (which is covered by LF008).

description: Governs the exercise of the High Court's inherent power to quash criminal proceedings at a preliminary stage by strictly evaluating whether the uncontroverted allegations prima facie constitute an offence without embarking on an evidentiary mini-trial.
application_scenario: Use when an accused petitions the High Court under Section 482 CrPC (or similar inherent jurisdiction) to quash an FIR, complaint, or cognizance order at the threshold, arguing that the allegations are absurd, legally barred, or do not disclose an offence.
reasoning_flow: Identify the invocation of inherent powers seeking premature termination of a criminal proceeding (e.g., quashing an FIR or cognizance order).
Examine the allegations in the FIR or complaint strictly at their face value, accepting them in their entirety for this limited analytical purpose.
Prohibit any meticulous appraisal of evidence, testing of witness reliability, or conducting of a mini-trial at this preliminary stage.

Quash the proceeding only if the uncontroverted allegations do not disclose any cognizable offence, or if there is an express legal bar; otherwise, dismiss the petition and allow the trial to proceed.
example_application: An accused seeks to quash an FIR for possessing a mobile phone in prison. The court examines the prison rules applicable on the date of the incident and finds mobile phones were not yet classified as prohibited articles. Without weighing evidence, the court quashes the FIR because, even if true, the allegations do not constitute a legal offence.
shared_pattern: All three cases deal with the threshold at which a High Court can exercise inherent powers to stop a criminal prosecution, emphasizing that proceedings can only be quashed if a facial reading of the allegations discloses no offence, barring any preliminary evidentiary evaluation.
scope_exclusions: Do not use for appeals against final acquittals or convictions after a full trial, or for regular appellate reappraisal of evidence.
